Press Release:


Three weeks after her term ended as Public Protector, Adv. Thuli Madonsela takes us through the State Capture Report which has thrust her back into the spotlight.

Script:


Bongani Bingwa: What kind of week have you had?
Adv. Madonsela: It’s my third week having finished my term as the Public Protector but I’m still starry eyed about my new life and all of the new things coming into my life, but of course it’s too early for my life to leave me alone, so part of the week has been to deal with some of the ghosts from my past.
Bingwa: You are obviously no longer the public protector but you still very much bare the brunt, certainly of your last report.
Madonsela: That is not shocking because usually with high stakes reports it does happen, it’s a pity that I had to release this one on my last day of work, which was not our plan but with the litigation that started shortly before we finalised and people not able to meet us on the day we had planned, it then forced us to roll the period right to the last day.
Bingwa: One of the criticisms has been that you concluded particularly the state capture report with some haste, and why did you not leave it to your successor to carry on and finalise?
Madonsela: I did conclude it with some haste. It was a report that should have been done with some haste, that’s a statutory requirement, I didn’t create that statute.
Bingwa: One of the objections that the President and his legal representatives have made is that they weren’t given sufficient time to respond to respond to the questions, to prepare for the questions that you had to bring to him.
Madonsela: Firstly we don’t give anybody sufficient time with the questions we give you sufficient time with the allegations against you. We gave the president sufficient time. My first letter to him was in March, I followed up with his office in the very same month of March to see if they had received it, we only discovered in April that they hadn’t received it and we sent another one on the 22nd of April, that is about 6 months of adequate notice that somebody is accusing you of having been in a room next door when they were being offered a job as a minister for gratification, which in other words is a corrupt offer, the Mentoor one. Also the Jonas thing, firstly the President was aware that Jonas had made this accusation and that it had been said that the people who made those offers to him were the Gupta family in the presence of his son. We gave him the notification.
Bingwa: What were some of the factual issues that you wanted the president to answer?
Madonsela: The first set of issues related to the relationship between the president and the Guptas and the relationship between the Guptas and his son and how that relationship started. The second set of questions relate to what he knew about the allegations made by these and what he did to deal with those allegations, because in terms of the law, he is required as the person with the sole executive authority in this country, to investigate any matter that arises as a suggestion of impropriety or irregularity. That is a responsibility he has under section 175 of the Constitution, it’s also the responsibility he has just generally as somebody who has to protect the Constitution.
Bingwa: So what do you make of Mr Molefe’s casual statement that he was not at the Guptas as often as it is suggested but that there is a Shebeen near by and he may have gone there.
Madonsela: I really don’t know and I’m in a bit of a difficulty because the Public Protector has issued a statement indicating that she would prefer to answer questions relating to the report herself and that journalists like yourself should ask those questions to her.
Bingwa: Perhaps in so far as it relates to the institution that may be fair, but a lot of the criticism has been levelled against you personally as the person who led the investigation. How have you reacted to some of those?
Madonsela: I think that criticism is unfair because even though I was team leader and even though the PP is both a person and an institution, Eskom should know that an investigation is done by the institution and an investigation team and that any insult to me, is an insult to the investigation team. Mr Molefe knows the truth, he knows that the evidence that we have at this stage shows that he has a relationship with the Gupta family but ofcourse the commission is still going to go deeper into it. What I would want him to do though when he deals with the commission is that he does better than he did in the public appearance yesterday.
Bingwa: You were not convinced?
Madonsela: I think in the public appearance he did two things that are normally associated with people who are prepped up for deflecting an issue, because he did two things, one was to vilify me and the company that used to have the contract with Eskom. The second thing was to paint himself as a victim. I didn’t hear Mr Molefe speak about I am friends with Mr Gupta which the evidence that we have at this stage, based on what Mr Gupta said is that they are friends. My Gupta said I regard him as my brother, we visit each others families. He also didn’t tell us that if it is true that they are friends how did he manage that conflict off interest in that process of dealing with Mr Gupta. He also didn’t tell the world why did he and Mr Ajay Gupta, phone each other more than 40 times.
Bingwa: It’s a fairly unusual recommendation for you to suggest that the Chief Justice nominate a judge that the president will appoint to head such a commission.
Madonsela: I still respect the fact that the President is the one who has the responsibility and right to appoint Commissions of Inquiry, but to make sure that we don’t run foul of the possibility of conflict of interest, he will still appoint, but he won’t select.
Bingwa: Adv. Madonsela has the South African state been captured?
Madonsela: We investigated what appeared to be improper relationships that are influencing appointments and the allocation of tenders and state affairs. At this stage I don’t think it’s proper to give you my personal views on it, it is better that we leave the commission of enquiry to say whether or not parts of the state, have been captured.

Promos
One x 10 sec
After seven years of being at the helm of one of the country’s most respected public institutions – Former Public Protector Adv. Thuli Madonsela sits down with Carte Blanche.
Two x 15 sec
VO: She’s one of the most celebrated public servants and after seven years in office, Adv. Thuli Madonsela reflects on her tenure.
UPSOUND: It went beyond my expectations, the opportunity to serve, the opportunity to make a difference in peoples lives.
Two x 15 sec
UPSOUND: One journalist told me that some of those whose cages have been rattled will follow me as a form of revenge. VO: It’s been three weeks since her term ended, but Former Public protector Adv. Thuli Madonsela is still feeling the heat.
